content: Enuresis, commonly referred to as bedwetting, affects up to 20% of five-year-old children and can have significant social, emotional, and psychological consequences. Treatment options include enuresis alarms, behavioral interventions, and pharmacological therapies. Enuresis alarms are devices that activate upon detecting urination, aiming to condition the child to wake up and use the bathroom. A systematic review of 74 trials involving 5,983 children aged 5 to 16 years assessed the effectiveness of enuresis alarms. At the end of treatment, enuresis alarms were found to reduce the number of wet nights per week compared to no treatment or control groups. Specifically, the mean difference (MD) in wet nights was −2.68 (95% confidence interval [CI] −4.59 to −0.78) based on low-quality evidence. Additionally, more children achieved a complete response (defined as 14 consecutive dry nights) with alarms compared to no treatment (relative risk [RR] 7.23, 95% CI 1.40 to 37.33; low-quality evidence). Furthermore, more children remained dry after treatment with alarms compared to no treatment (RR 9.67, 95% CI 4.74 to 19.76; low-quality evidence). When compared to placebo drugs, alarms may result in more children achieving a complete response (RR 1.59, 95% CI 1.16 to 2.17; low-quality evidence). However, there was no clear difference in the number of wet nights per week between alarms and placebo drugs (MD −0.96, 95% CI −2.32 to 0.41; very low-quality evidence). No trials comparing alarms to placebo drugs reported the number of children who remained dry after treatment. Code-word alarms, a variation of standard alarms, may slightly increase the number of children achieving a complete response at the end of treatment compared to standard alarms (RR 1.11, 95% CI 0.97 to 1.27; moderate-quality evidence). However, there was likely little to no difference in the number of children remaining dry post-treatment between code-word alarms and standard alarms (RR 0.91, 95% CI 0.79 to 1.05; moderate-quality evidence). The effectiveness of other types of alarms compared to standard alarms remains uncertain due to very low-quality evidence. When compared to behavioral interventions such as waking routines, bladder training, dry-bed training, or reward systems, alarms may reduce the number of wet nights per week (MD −0.81, 95% CI −2.01 to 0.38; low-quality evidence). Alarms may also increase the number of children achieving a complete response (RR 1.77, 95% CI 0.98 to 3.19; low-quality evidence) and slightly increase the number of children remaining dry post-treatment (RR 1.39, 95% CI 0.81 to 2.41; low-quality evidence). When compared to desmopressin, a commonly used pharmacological treatment, alarms showed low-quality evidence of a small reduction in wet nights per week (MD −0.64, 95% CI −1.77 to 0.49). The number of children achieving a complete response at the end of treatment was similar between alarms and desmopressin (RR 1.12, 95% CI 0.93 to 1.36; low-quality evidence). However, alarms may slightly increase the number of children remaining dry post-treatment compared to desmopressin (RR 1.30, 95% CI 0.92 to 1.84; moderate-quality evidence). The comparison between alarms and tricyclic antidepressants showed very low-quality evidence, making it uncertain whether there are differences in the number of wet nights, complete responses, or post-treatment dryness. Similarly, the effectiveness of alarms compared to cognitive behavioral therapy, psychotherapy, hypnotherapy, or restricted diets remains unclear due to very low-quality evidence. Combining alarms with desmopressin may reduce the number of wet nights per week compared to desmopressin alone (MD −0.88, 95% CI −1.38 to −0.38; low-quality evidence). This combination may also increase the number of children achieving a complete response (RR 1.32, 95% CI 1.08 to 1.62; low-quality evidence) and the number of children remaining dry post-treatment (RR 2.33, 95% CI 1.26 to 4.29; low-quality evidence). Similarly, combining alarms with dry-bed training may increase the number of children achieving a complete response compared to dry-bed training alone (RR 3.79, 95% CI 1.85 to 7.77; low-quality evidence). However, it is unclear whether this combination improves post-treatment dryness due to wide confidence intervals (RR 0.56, 95% CI 0.15 to 2.12; low-quality evidence). The effectiveness of combining alarms with bladder training compared to bladder training alone is also uncertain due to very low-quality evidence. Adverse events were reported in 17 of the 74 trials, while nine trials reported no adverse events, and 48 trials did not mention adverse events. Adverse events associated with alarms included failure to wake the child, false alarms (ringing without urination), waking others in the household, causing discomfort, frightening the child, and being too difficult to use. Adverse events associated with comparator interventions included nosebleeds, headaches, and abdominal pain. Code-word alarms may slightly increase adverse events compared to standard alarms (RR 1.34, 95% CI 0.75 to 2.38; moderate-quality evidence), although the wide confidence interval introduces uncertainty. Alarms likely reduce the number of children experiencing adverse events compared to desmopressin (RR 0.38, 95% CI 0.20 to 0.71; moderate-quality evidence). However, due to very low-quality evidence, it is unclear whether the adverse event rate for alarms is lower than for other treatments. In conclusion, enuresis alarms may be more effective than no treatment in reducing bedwetting in children. While the evidence comparing alarms to desmopressin is uncertain, alarms likely have a lower risk of adverse events than desmopressin. Despite the large number of trials included in this review, further well-designed and adequately powered studies are needed to fully determine the effectiveness of alarm therapy.
